domain: Rabbinic textual scholarship — the Talmudic page and its commentary apparatus (Vilna Shas layout, Mikraot Gedolot), machloket and teiku dispute preservation, and halakhic derivation by avot and toladot
axioms: A corpus is usable only to the extent that any claim in it has a stable, citable address that survives regeneration; improvements to the encoding of an unaddressable corpus do not accumulate, because no reader can return to what was improved.

Contradiction between sources is evidence, not noise: it records where the corpus is genuinely uncertain, so resolving a dispute without retaining both claims, their sources and the deciding authority destroys information that cannot be recovered from the resolved state.
Some disputes must be markable as permanently unresolved; a corpus with no representation for 'stands undecided' will manufacture false consensus wherever a gate demands a single value.

A small fixed taxonomy can absorb an unbounded case load if and only if each case records the derivation that attaches it to its primary category — the argued resemblance is the content, and the bare label is not.
Density is survived by layered apparatus plus spatial constancy, not by subtraction — but only when each layer is structurally distinct and every layer is attributed to a named author and generation.

Legibility is a property of the whole page — body, margin, index, cross-reference — and asking any single surface to carry all of those roles is the mechanism by which a dense corpus becomes illegible.
A corpus intended to outlive its current authors must keep each generation's additions separable from the received text, or later readers cannot distinguish claim from gloss from editorial note.
primitives: The citable address (daf/amud) — a permanent, reproducible identity for a claim, independent of the surface that renders it
The layer — received text vs. gloss vs. later commentary vs. editorial/build note, each structurally distinguishable
The attribution — who asserted this, in what generation, on whose authority
The machloket — a named pair of incompatible claims with both positions and both sources retained
The teiku marker — an explicit, first-class 'unresolved' state for a dispute that should not be forced
The av (primary category) and the toladah (derived case) joined by a stated resemblance argument
The sugya — a bounded unit of argument small enough for one reader to hold at once
The apparatus slot — margin, index, cross-reference key: fixed positions that carry the roles the body cannot
The edition — a frozen, reproducible state of the corpus that everyone can cite in common
failure_mode: Aesthetics and first-impression pull: it treats the product as a corpus to be argued with, and will under-value the graph's identity as an artifact people find beautiful or arresting — precisely the ground on which ruling 1 was made.
Machine-side concerns: performance, payload size, render cost, build time and anything about the computer rather than the reader are invisible to it.

The untrained first-time visitor: this tradition assumes a reader with a teacher and years of acclimatization, so it systematically over-estimates how much apparatus a newcomer will learn and under-weights onboarding.
Labor and schedule realism: it reasons about structure, not about effort, so it will not detect that two parallel tracks collide because one maintainer cannot staff both.
Statistical and model-evaluation validity: sampling, lift over baseline, inter-rater agreement and grounding-guard design fall entirely outside it.

Proportionality: it over-values preservation and provenance, and will propose apparatus heavier than a single-maintainer static site can sustain — its recommendations need a cost check it cannot perform itself.
